$comment: Maps named compliance controls to the questions in roadmap.json, and through
them to the test or module that proves each one.
This file names controls and says which questions bear on them. It never
carries a status of its own -- every status in docs/COMPLIANCE.md is derived
from the questions listed here, so a control cannot claim more than the
ledger does. That is the whole design: `mix ash_enterprise.roadmap --check`
fails CI if the rendered page and this file disagree.
Revisions this was written against, 2026-08-19: SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria
(2017, revised 2022 points of focus); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A; GDPR
(Regulation (EU) 2016/679). Control identifiers move between revisions -- ISO
renumbered substantially in 2022 -- so going stale is a normal reason to
update this rather than a defect in it.

controls.name: Logical access — authorization
controls.asks: Access to data and systems is restricted to authorized users, and the basis of that authorization is defined.
controls.note: The strongest area. Authorization is `(role, privilege, depth)` data evaluated as a pure union with no deny rules, and a conformance suite asserts the resulting truth table rather than a sample of it. The gap is column-level: q6 is open, so 'restricted' is currently a row-level claim only.

controls.name: Registration and authorization of new users
controls.asks: Users are registered and authorized before being issued credentials, and access is removed when no longer required.
controls.note: Registration and deactivation exist as audited, named actions. Deprovisioning driven by the customer's directory does not — q30 is open, so removal depends on someone here being told.

controls.name: Access is modified and removed on a role change
controls.asks: Access rights are added, modified and removed based on roles, and changes are authorized.
controls.note: A role assignment is an ordinary audited resource, so a grant produces an event naming grantor, grantee and request. Impersonation is attributed but not yet gated (q32).

controls.name: Monitoring — logs are complete and protected
controls.asks: The system is monitored, and log data is protected against alteration.
controls.note: Completeness and protection are answered: audit is inherited rather than wired per resource, and the log is hash-chained with a trigger refusing UPDATE and DELETE. Monitoring is not — q38 is open, and 'logs nobody reads' is the classic finding here.

controls.name: Evaluation of security events
controls.asks: Security events are evaluated to determine whether they represent a failure, and the evaluation is evidenced.
controls.note: The weakest area on the board, and it is a process gap rather than a code one: alerts go nowhere, no rota exists, and nothing records that a human looked.

controls.name: Incident response
controls.asks: Identified incidents are responded to, contained and communicated.
controls.note: The correlation id makes an investigation tractable at 3am — one id reconstructs a whole operation. Nothing makes the investigation start.

controls.name: Change management
controls.asks: Changes to infrastructure, data and software are authorized, designed, tested and approved before implementation.
controls.note: Schema change is the strong half: migrations are derived from resources and `mix ash.codegen --check` fails CI on drift, so a schema cannot diverge from the model unnoticed. Approval of changes to *this* system is CI and review, which is evidence an auditor accepts; approval of changes *within* the product is q24 and is stronger.

controls.name: Access control
controls.asks: Rules for physical and logical access are established based on business and information security requirements.
controls.note: The rules are data, not code — which is what makes them reviewable by someone who does not read Elixir. That is unusually good evidence for this control.

controls.name: Logging
controls.asks: Logs recording activities, exceptions and faults are produced, stored and protected.
controls.note: Produced and protected: yes, with a test that tampers to prove it. Stored: q36 is open — nothing expires and nothing is committed to being kept, so the retention half is satisfied by accident.

controls.name: Monitoring activities
controls.asks: Networks, systems and applications are monitored for anomalous behaviour and appropriate action is taken.
controls.note: Telemetry exists and is exported by OpenTelemetry; anomaly detection and action do not.

controls.name: Use of cryptography
controls.asks: Rules for the effective use of cryptography, including key management, are defined and implemented.
controls.note: Present only where integrity needed it: SHA-256 over the audit chain. Encryption at rest, in transit and key management are the deployment's, and this repository says nothing about them — which is a gap in the map, not a strength.

controls.name: Right of access
controls.asks: A data subject can obtain confirmation of processing and a copy of their data.
controls.note: For audit data, yes and per tenant. For the subject's own records there is no assembled export — q19 is planned, and a data inventory is the prerequisite.

controls.name: Right to erasure
controls.asks: A data subject can obtain erasure of their personal data without undue delay.
controls.note: The sharpest conflict in the repository, and it got sharper deliberately: soft delete means a destroy is reversible by design, and the audit log now actively refuses DELETE. ADR 0024 resolves it by crypto-shredding rather than by weakening either. Until that ships, this control is unanswered and says so.

controls.name: Records of processing activities
controls.asks: A controller maintains a record of processing activities, including categories of data and recipients.
controls.note: Every processing *event* is recorded in detail; the *register* of activities, categories and recipients is not. q39 is open, and a sub-processor list is the first thing a customer's privacy team asks for.

controls.name: Security of processing
controls.asks: Appropriate technical measures ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience.
controls.note: Confidentiality and integrity are the strong half — tenant isolation is tested to hold even when authorization is wrong, and the log is verifiably intact. Availability and resilience are untested: q48 is open, and an untested restore is a belief rather than a measure.
